title: Wren and the Portrait
premise: Rafael Iversen, a property surveyor hired to appraise his late grandmother's house, discovers that every photograph taken inside now contains an extra chair—and in the oldest portrait, a girl named Wren has turned her head since he last looked. The house appraises back: it measures him, room by room, and offers belonging at the price of his name, his reflection, and eventually his face. To escape before the well beneath the kitchen refills and drowns the property in memory, Rafael must learn the lullaby's final verse from Wren herself without ever singing along—because everyone who sings it becomes part of the house's collection. In the end Rafael trades his own portrait for Wren's freedom, walks out nameless into the morning, and lets the house keep the chair that was always meant for him.
about_author: Mirabel Brightwater is the pen name of a former estate appraiser who spent eleven years cataloguing houses no one would buy twice. She writes horror in a converted schoolhouse she refuses to photograph.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Rafael arrives at the inherited Iversen house with a clipboard and twenty years of practiced rationality, measuring rooms for probate. POV: Rafael. The beat is uneasy competence—every measurement comes out one inch longer on the second try.

chapters.title: Extra Seating
chapters.summary: Sorting grandma's photographs, Rafael finds an unfamiliar wooden chair appearing in pictures spanning six decades, always closer to the camera. POV: Rafael. The beat is denial curdling into dread as he counts chairs in the dining room: twelve photographed, thirteen present.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: In the attic, Rafael finds a portrait of a girl labeled 'Wren, 1911' whose eyes have moved since yesterday. She speaks without moving her mouth, asking if he's come to stay. POV: Rafael. The beat is the collapse of explanation—the first honest fear of his adult life.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: Rafael tries to leave; the road loops back to the porch. A neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, warns him: finish the appraisal, learn the song, never sing along. POV: Rafael. The beat is grim acceptance—he begins taking notes like the surveyor he is.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms
chapters.summary: Rafael catalogs the house systematically, discovering each room 'appraises' him—showing what he'd surrender to belong there. The bathroom shows his reflection aging decades in seconds. POV: Rafael. The beat is clinical detachment failing against personal grief.

chapters.title: The Well Beneath
chapters.summary: Under the kitchen floor, Rafael finds a stone well, dry but rising, humming the lullaby's first two verses. Mrs. Okafor explains the house refills when it chooses a new resident. POV: Rafael. The beat is urgency—the deadline made physical.

chapters.title: Grandma's Ledger
chapters.summary: In grandma's papers, Rafael learns she was the last to refuse the song, holding the house off for sixty years by paying smaller prices: her sister, her voice, her Sundays. POV: mixed—Rafael reading, grandma's letters in italics. The beat is horrified love.

chapters.title: What the Chair Remembers
chapters.summary: Rafael sits in the thirteenth chair and experiences Wren's 1911: a child promised to the house by parents fleeing debt. He wakes with sawdust under his nails. POV: split Rafael/Wren. The beat is empathy replacing terror.

chapters.title: First Verse
chapters.summary: The well refills ankle-deep overnight. Rafael transcribes the lullaby from the walls, which sweat musical notation. Singing even silently makes the house warm toward him. POV: Rafael. The beat is temptation—the house feels more like home than anywhere he's rented.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okafor's Price
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okafor reveals she once lived here; her missing left hand paid for her exit. She teaches Rafael the rule: the last verse can only be learned from someone the house still holds. POV: Mrs. Okafor flashback, then Rafael. The beat is mentorship shadowed by sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Collection
chapters.summary: Rafael explores the cellar and finds portraits of every previous resident, each face subtly becoming the house's style—his grandmother's among them, smiling wrong. POV: Rafael. The beat is identity horror: belonging here means being repainted.

chapters.title: Knee-Deep
chapters.summary: The well reaches Rafael's knees; the water tastes like childhood. His reflection in dark windows starts sitting in the extra chair before he does. POV: Rafael. The beat is erosion—he can't remember his apartment's color anymore.

chapters.title: Negotiation
chapters.summary: Rafael attempts to appraise the house itself, offering a formal valuation in exchange for release. The house counters: one portrait, freely given. POV: Rafael. The beat is desperate bargaining—he doesn't yet understand what a portrait costs.

chapters.title: Wren's Verse
chapters.summary: Wren, able to approach only where the wallpaper peels, teaches Rafael the third verse through the gap, warning him the fourth exists nowhere written. POV: alternating Rafael/Wren. The beat is fragile alliance—two prisoners teaching each other escape routes.

chapters.title: The House Makes Its Offer
chapters.summary: The house floods the upstairs with warmth: cooked meals, mended clothes, a chair fitted exactly to Rafael's body. It shows him a life where he never leaves, never lacks. POV: Rafael. The beat is the seduction at its peak—survival versus surrender.

chapters.title: Sediment
chapters.summary: Rafael catches himself humming verse two and tears his own thumbnail trying to stop. His handwriting is changing; his signature won't hold its shape. POV: Rafael. The beat is self-alienation—he is becoming furniture that walks.

chapters.title: Chest-Deep
chapters.summary: The well rises past his chest while he sleeps. Mrs. Okafor breaks in and pulls him out, losing her remaining hand to the doorframe's price. POV: Rafael. The beat is guilt and gratitude—the cost others pay for your survival.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse
chapters.summary: Wren confesses she knows the final verse because the house composed it through her—but anyone who hears it whole must answer it. She offers to sing it alone so Rafael only overhears. POV: Wren. The beat is sacrifice offered, refused.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: The well crests. The house stops pretending: doors become mouths, hallways become throat. Rafael runs the appraisal route one last time, memorizing the house as it tries to memorize him. POV: Rafael. The beat is clarity through extremity.

chapters.title: The Portrait Given
chapters.summary: At the well's edge, Rafael paints his own portrait—faceless, nameless—and gives it freely, satisfying the counter-offer. The house accepts the shape of him instead of the substance. POV: Rafael. The beat is costly agency: paying with identity to keep the soul.

chapters.title: Last Verse, Unsung
chapters.summary: As the well drains, Wren sings the fourth verse over Rafael's silence; he learns it by hearing, holds it by not returning it. Her portrait empties. She steps out ninety years late, blinking at daylight. POV: Rafael and Wren together. The beat is release—the price paid, the debt closed.

chapters.title: Appraised at Nothing
chapters.summary: Rafael signs the house's final valuation—zero, condemned—and walks out beside Wren, nameless but unowned. Behind them, the thirteenth chair rocks once and settles. POV: Rafael, closing on Wren seeing sky. The beat is bittersweet belonging: they have nothing, and it is finally theirs.
